section.title: Asa's Later Years
section.sectionRationale: The same Asa who once cried out to the LORD against Zerah's million man army now, decades later, faces a lesser threat from Baasha of Israel and instead pays Ben-hadad of Aram to break his treaty and attack Israel from the north. The seer Hanani rebukes him for relying on a foreign king rather than the LORD, and Asa, enraged, imprisons the seer and oppresses some of the people. Even his final illness becomes another test: diseased in his feet, Asa seeks only physicians and not the LORD, and dies in the forty-first year of his reign.
section.thesis: Asa's tragic decline shows that a heart once fully devoted can still drift into relying on human alliances rather than God, and that resisting correction only compounds the failure, a sober warning that yesterday's faith in crisis does not automatically secure today's faithfulness.
section.frameNote: Three beats: Asa's alliance with Ben-hadad against Baasha, verses 1 to 6; Hanani's rebuke and Asa's rage, verses 7 to 10; and Asa's illness, death, and burial, verses 11 to 14.

units.label: Asa's alliance with Ben-hadad against Baasha
units.note: silver and gold from the treasuries

verses.text: In the thirty-sixth year of Asa's reign, Baasha king of Israel went up against Judah and fortified Ramah to prevent anyone from leaving or entering the territory of Asa king of Judah.
So Asa withdrew the silver and gold from the treasuries of the house of the LORD and the royal palace, and he sent it with this message to Ben-hadad king of Aram, who was ruling in Damascus:

"Let there be a {{beritCovenant|treaty}} between me and you as there was between my father and your father. See, I have sent you silver and gold. Now go and break your treaty with Baasha king of Israel, so that he will withdraw from me."
And Ben-hadad listened to King Asa and sent the commanders of his armies against the cities of Israel, conquering Ijon, Dan, Abel-maim, and all the store cities of Naphtali.
When Baasha learned of this, he stopped fortifying Ramah and abandoned his work.
Then King Asa brought all the men of Judah, and they carried away the stones of Ramah and the timbers Baasha had used for building. And with these materials he built up Geba and Mizpah.

At that time Hanani the seer came to King Asa of Judah and told him, "Because you have relied on the king of Aram and not on the LORD your God, the army of the king of Aram has escaped from your hand.
Were not the Cushites and Libyans a vast army with many chariots and horsemen? Yet because you {{samak|relied}} on the LORD, He delivered them into your hand.

For the {{ayin|eyes}} of the LORD roam to and fro over all the earth, to show Himself strong on behalf of those whose hearts are fully devoted to Him. You have acted foolishly in this matter. From now on, therefore, you will be at war."
Asa was angry with the seer and became so enraged over this matter that he put the man in prison. And at the same time Asa oppressed some of the people.

units.label: Asa's illness, death, and burial
units.note: he sought the physicians, not the LORD

verses.text: Now the acts of Asa, from beginning to end, are indeed written in the Book of the Kings of Judah and Israel.

In the thirty-ninth year of his reign, Asa became diseased in his feet, and his disease became increasingly severe. Yet even in his illness he did not seek the LORD, but only the {{rapha|physicians}}.
So in the forty-first year of his reign, Asa died and rested with his fathers.

And he was buried in the tomb that he had cut out for himself in the City of David. They laid him on a bier that was full of spices and various blended perfumes; then they made a great fire in his honor.

beritCovenant.gloss: Covenant, treaty. Asa appeals to a berit that had existed between his father and Ben-hadad's father, a political treaty he now revives with a foreign king rather than renewing his own earlier covenant to seek the LORD, chapter 15, a telling substitution of one kind of covenant for another.

samak.gloss: To rely, lean upon. Hanani's rebuke pointedly recalls that Asa once samak, relied, on the LORD against the vast Cushite army, chapter 14, making his present reliance on Ben-hadad instead of God an especially foolish and inexcusable contrast with his own earlier faith.

ayin.gloss: Eye, eyes. Hanani declares that the ayin of the LORD roam over all the earth to show Himself strong for those whose hearts are fully devoted, a vivid image of God's constant, searching attentiveness, making Asa's failure to rely on Him not a matter of God's absence but of Asa's own misplaced trust.

rapha.gloss: To heal; here used of physicians, those who practice healing. The text's pointed contrast, he did not seek the LORD but only the rapha, physicians, does not condemn medical care itself but names the deeper failure, that even in mortal illness Asa's instinct was to seek human help alone rather than first seeking God.

basic.context: Decades after relying wholly on the LORD against an overwhelming Cushite army, Asa faces a much smaller threat from Baasha of Israel and responds very differently, stripping the temple and palace treasuries to bribe Ben-hadad of Aram into breaking his own treaty and attacking Israel from the north. It works militarily, but the seer Hanani confronts Asa, reminding him that relying on the LORD once brought total victory over impossible odds, so relying on Aram now was foolish, especially since the LORD's eyes search the whole earth to strengthen the fully devoted. Rather than repenting, Asa imprisons Hanani and oppresses some of the people. Two years later, diseased in his feet, Asa again seeks help everywhere except from the LORD, turning only to physicians, and dies soon after.
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative recording a specific political and personal decline late in an otherwise faithful king's reign; it is not a blanket condemnation of medical treatment or foreign diplomacy as such. What is theologically significant is the contrast the Chronicler draws deliberately between the younger Asa who relied on God against impossible odds and the older Asa who relied on human alliances against a lesser threat and then hardened his heart against correction, showing that past faithfulness does not guarantee present faithfulness.
basic.originalLanguages: Asa revives a political berit, treaty, with Aram rather than his own earlier covenant to seek the LORD, prompting Hanani's rebuke that he once samak, relied, on God but now does not. Hanani insists the LORD's ayin, eyes, roam the whole earth seeking whom to strengthen, making Asa's choice inexcusable, and the narrative's final indictment is that in his illness Asa sought only the rapha, physicians, never turning back to the LORD.
basic.typology: Asa's earlier reliance on God against Zerah, followed by his later reliance on Ben-hadad against Baasha, previews the church's ongoing temptation to trust worldly alliances rather than Christ, and Hanani's imprisonment for speaking truth anticipates the rejection faithful prophetic voices, and ultimately Christ Himself, would repeatedly suffer at the hands of those they confronted. Asa's refusal to seek the LORD even in mortal illness contrasts with Christ, the true Physician who is Himself sought first and who heals both body and soul.
basic.christ: Hanani's declaration that the LORD's eyes roam the earth to strengthen the fully devoted anticipates Christ's own promise that the Father sees in secret and rewards genuine faith, and stands as a rebuke to every substitute reliance on worldly power rather than on God. Asa's tragic refusal to seek the LORD in illness contrasts sharply with Christ, the true and greater Physician who welcomes the sick who come to Him first, rather than last, for healing of both body and soul, Mark 2:17.
basic.god: God remains faithful and ready to show Himself strong for those whose hearts are fully devoted to Him, His eyes searching all the earth for such people. Yet He does not force reliance on Himself, and He allows the consequences of misplaced trust, war rather than the peace faithful reliance had once secured, to unfold as both discipline and warning, even for a king who had once known His deliverance firsthand.
basic.crossReferences: 1 Kings 15:16-24 gives the parallel account of Asa's conflict with Baasha and alliance with Ben-hadad. 2 Chronicles 14:9-13 records Asa's earlier, contrasting reliance on the LORD against Zerah. 2 Chronicles 16:9's declaration that God's eyes roam the earth echoes Zechariah 4:10. And Mark 2:17 shows Christ as the true physician who calls sinners, not the healthy, to seek Him.
basic.oneStory: The same Asa who once cried out to the LORD against impossible odds later relies on a foreign king against a lesser threat, and when confronted, hardens his heart rather than repenting, even seeking only physicians rather than God in his final illness. This sober decline warns every believer that past faithfulness must be renewed daily, and it points forward to Christ, the true Physician and object of unwavering trust, whom Asa's story urges every reader to seek first, in crisis and in health alike.

context.literary:
The chapter is built as a deliberate mirror of chapter 14. There Asa faced an overwhelming Cushite army and cried out, LORD, there is no one besides You to help the mighty and the weak, 2 Chronicles 14:11, and won outright. Here he faces a comparatively minor threat, a single northern king fortifying a border town, and instead strips the temple treasury to buy foreign intervention. Hanani's rebuke in verse 8 makes the mirroring explicit, naming the earlier Cushite victory specifically so the contrast cannot be missed.

The narrative then tightens into a spiral rather than a simple sequence: alliance, verses 1 to 6, rebuke, verses 7 to 9, rage, verse 10, and finally an unrepentant illness and death, verses 11 to 14, each stage narrower and darker than the one before it. Even the closing regnal formula breaks the pattern typical of faithful kings elsewhere in Chronicles; rather than closing on praise, it closes on the flat, damning note that Asa sought only physicians, never the LORD.

The verb withdrew in verse 2, describing Asa taking silver and gold out of the temple treasuries, deserves notice for what it is not; the previous chapter records Asa himself bringing dedicated wealth into the house of God. Here the direction of movement reverses, wealth leaves the temple to purchase a foreign king's help, a small but telling narrative signal of where Asa's trust has now shifted.
context.historical:
Ramah sat only a few miles north of Jerusalem astride the main road connecting Judah to the north, and a fortified Ramah in Baasha's hands could choke off trade and pilgrim traffic into the capital, which explains the urgency behind Asa's response even though Baasha commanded nowhere near the numbers Zerah once had. Ben-hadad ruled from Damascus as one in a line of Aramean kings who used that same throne name across generations, so this Ben-hadad should not be assumed identical with the later Ben-hadad who besieges Samaria in Elisha's day.

The thirty sixth year of Asa's reign, verse 1, creates a genuine chronological puzzle, since 1 Kings 16:8 places Baasha's own death around Asa's twenty sixth year, well before this conflict could have occurred if the years are counted from Asa's own accession. Many historians resolve this by reading such years as counted from the division of the kingdom under Rehoboam rather than from each king's individual accession, a reckoning convention that appears at points elsewhere in Chronicles and would place this conflict correctly within Baasha's actual lifetime.

Hanani's own family reappears across the following chapters in a way worth tracing; his son Jehu later confronts Asa's own son Jehoshaphat for an almost identical failure, allying with a compromised northern king, 2 Chronicles 19:2, a striking detail suggesting one prophetic household held two successive kings of Judah to the very same standard, father and son alike, across a single generational span.
context.canonical:
This chapter parallels 1 Kings 15:16 to 24 closely for the political narrative, but Hanani's confrontation and its aftermath, verses 7 to 10, belong entirely to the Chronicler, part of his consistent habit of supplying the prophetic commentary Kings leaves out, explaining not just what happened but why it mattered before God.

Hanani himself is not a new figure invented for this scene; 1 Kings 16:1 and 7 names his son Jehu as a prophet active under Baasha's own successor, and Chronicles later shows that same Jehu confronting Jehoshaphat, 2 Chronicles 19:2, and eventually contributing material to the royal records, 2 Chronicles 20:34. A single prophetic family, it turns out, spans and critiques an entire stretch of Judah's kings, father confronting Asa, son confronting Asa's own heir, for strikingly similar failures of misplaced trust.

The chapter's central charge, that Asa relied, samak, on Aram rather than on the LORD, becomes something of a refrain across the rest of the book; later kings are repeatedly measured by exactly this question, where their trust actually rested in a crisis, Ahaz turning to Assyria, 2 Chronicles 28:16 to 21, or Hezekiah refusing to turn anywhere but the LORD, 2 Chronicles 32:7 to 8. Asa's later failure becomes the template the Chronicler holds up as the wrong answer every time the same test recurs for a later king.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The Chronicler is not merely recording political history; he is holding up Asa's own biography as a warning shaped for readers who might otherwise assume that a single great act of faith settles the matter permanently. Asa cried out to the LORD against impossible odds in chapter 14 and is never called into question for it; the same king, decades later, faces far better odds and fails the same basic test, reliance. By placing these two moments in deliberate tension, the author wants his postexilic readers, themselves tempted to look back on Israel's history and assume their own community's earlier faithfulness settled the question once for all, to understand that reliance on God has to be renewed in every fresh crisis, not banked like an account balance.

The account of Hanani's imprisonment carries a second, sharper intent, to show that resisting correction compounds a failure rather than containing it, since Asa's rage against a faithful messenger, and his oppression of others, verse 10, only deepens the very isolation from God that started the decline.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Nothing in this chapter forbids medical treatment or foreign diplomacy as categories; Scripture elsewhere assumes both are legitimate, a physician named Luke travels with Paul, Colossians 4:14, and treaties between nations are not inherently condemned. What the narrative actually targets is exclusivity, seeking physicians or foreign kings instead of the LORD rather than alongside continued trust in Him. Asa's fault was not that he sought help but that help fully displaced God from the picture, in the war and again in his final illness.

What carries forward as binding instruction is the priority such episodes demand, that every legitimate means of help, medical, diplomatic, or otherwise, remains subordinate to reliance on God rather than a replacement for it, and that correction, however unwelcome, should be received with humility rather than met with the anger and imprisonment Asa turned on Hanani.

debates.question: Does verse 12's report that Asa sought only the physicians, not the LORD, condemn medical treatment as such?

views.label: No, it condemns exclusive reliance, not medicine itself
views.case: Elsewhere Scripture assumes the legitimacy of medical care without censure, Luke the physician travels with Paul, Colossians 4:14, so the text's complaint is precisely the word only, that Asa sought physicians instead of the LORD rather than in addition to Him.

views.label: It may reflect medicine's ancient entanglement with pagan practice
views.case: Physicians in the wider ancient Near East often blended treatment with divination or appeals to foreign gods, so Asa's turn to physicians rather than the LORD could describe a turn toward compromised, syncretistic healing practices specifically, not medical care as modern readers understand it.

debates.bearing: Either reading agrees the core failure is exclusion, God shut out entirely, rather than the mere presence of human help alongside Him.

debates.question: How should the thirty sixth year of Asa's reign, verse 1, be reconciled with Baasha's death recorded earlier in 1 Kings 16:8?

views.label: Years reckoned from the division of the kingdom
views.case: If the years in this section count from the split under Rehoboam rather than from each king's own accession, the conflict falls correctly within Baasha's actual reign, a reckoning convention some historians find used elsewhere in these chapters.

views.label: A numeral difficulty in transmission
views.case: Some scholars propose the number has simply been corrupted somewhere in the copying of the text, perhaps confusing a sixteenth year with a thirty sixth, since the surrounding events fit far more naturally earlier in Asa's reign.

debates.bearing: Whichever explanation is correct, the theological point the Chronicler is making, that Asa's later years show a marked decline from his earlier faith, does not depend on resolving the exact date.

study.originalLanguages:
The treaty Asa proposes to Ben-hadad in verse 3 is called a berit, using the very word for covenant that anchored the previous chapter's solemn national commitment to the LORD. The repetition is not accidental; Asa is shown reaching for a berit with a foreign king built on silver and gold rather than renewing the berit his own nation had so recently sworn on oath, a substitution of one kind of binding relationship for another that the narrative lets the reader notice without needing to state it outright.

Hanani's rebuke turns on the verb samak, relied, a word that pictures leaning one's whole weight on something, used here first of Asa's earlier posture toward the Cushite army, verse 8, and then, by implication, of his present posture toward Aram. The same root describes hands pressed down in blessing or ordination elsewhere in the Torah, Numbers 27:18, carrying a sense of full, weight bearing dependence rather than casual trust.

Verse 9's image of the LORD's eyes roaming, meshotetot, to and fro across all the earth uses a participle built from a root associated with restless movement or patrol, the same verb used of the four chariots patrolling the whole earth in Zechariah's vision, Zechariah 6:7, a picture less of passive observation than of active, searching reconnaissance for anyone whose heart is fully devoted.

Asa's anger in verse 10 is described with the verb qatsaph, a strong term for fury rather than mere irritation, the same root Scripture uses of the LORD's own wrath against covenant breakers, Numbers 16:22, so that the text quietly lets readers feel the intensity of Asa's reaction, a wrath fitting a wronged party rather than a corrected one.

Finally, in verse 12, the narrator says Asa did not darash, seek, the LORD, using the identical verb that carried the entire covenant of the previous chapter, seek and be found. Its negation here is the chapter's quiet verdict, the very word that defined Asa's finest hour now appears only to describe its absence in his last one, closing his reign with the standard formula that he rested with his fathers, shakab im avotav, the same idiom Scripture uses for every king's death, faithful or not, a reminder that this ordinary ending closes an extraordinary reign. Even Hanani's own title varies the point; he is called a seer, chozeh, rather than a prophet, navi, a related but distinct term for one who perceives rather than merely speaks, and it is precisely that perceiving Asa refuses to receive.

typology.type: Asa's earlier total reliance on the LORD against Zerah, later replaced by reliance on Ben-hadad against a lesser threat, chapters 14 and 16
typology.fulfillment: The contrast pictures a danger that stalks every believer, not the collapse of faith all at once but its quiet substitution, trusting God fully in the largest crises while reaching for merely human security in smaller ones. Paul's warning to the Galatians, having begun by the Spirit, are you now being perfected by the flesh, Galatians 3:3, names the same pattern in different terms. The type is a warning rather than a promise, and it falls short of Christ entirely, since He never once shifted His trust away from the Father, even facing a burden far heavier than Ramah.

typology.type: Hanani imprisoned for delivering a true, unwelcome word, verse 10
typology.fulfillment: A faithful messenger pays a real price simply for refusing to soften what God actually said, a pattern that recurs throughout the prophets and reaches its full weight in Christ, who was struck, mocked, and finally killed for speaking exactly what the Father gave Him to say, John 8:40. The correspondence is real, truth costing the truth teller something, but it also falls short, since Hanani's imprisonment ends in silence while Christ's death becomes, through the resurrection, the very means by which His word finally triumphs rather than being suppressed.

typology.type: Asa seeking physicians but not the LORD in his final illness, verse 12
typology.fulfillment: A king with every resource available still manages to shut God out of the one crisis that finally kills him, choosing help without the Helper. Christ stands as the direct reversal of that failure, the true physician who invites the sick to come to Him first rather than last, it is not the healthy who need a physician, but the sick, Mark 2:17. Where Asa sought healing apart from God, Christ offers Himself as healing that cannot be separated from God, since He is God present to heal both body and soul together.

typology.type: Withdrawing silver and gold from the temple treasury to purchase Aram's help, verse 2
typology.fulfillment: What had been dedicated to God is redirected to buy a substitute security, temple wealth spent to secure what trust in the LORD alone was meant to secure freely. It anticipates, faintly, the later stripping of the temple under unfaithful kings like Ahaz, 2 Chronicles 28:21, and stands against Christ, who instead of taking from what is holy for His own safety, gave up everything that was rightfully His so that others could be made rich, 2 Corinthians 8:9.

study.christ:
Hanani's declaration that the LORD's eyes roam the whole earth to show Himself strong for the fully devoted anticipates Christ's own teaching that the Father who sees in secret rewards what is done in secret, Matthew 6:4 and 6, the same conviction that God's attention is neither distant nor selective but searches actively for genuine devotion wherever it exists, now voiced by the Son who claims to know the Father's own searching heart firsthand, John 10:15.

The chapter also reaches Christ through contrast rather than direct promise. Asa, decades removed from his own finest hour, reaches for a foreign king's help and hardens against correction when confronted; Christ, tested far more severely and far more often, never once reaches for an alternative to the Father's will, not even when offered every kingdom of the world for the taking, Matthew 4:8 to 10. Where Asa's later years show devotion eroding under smaller and smaller pressures, Christ's own obedience only deepens as the pressure increases, culminating in Gethsemane's not my will but Yours, Luke 22:42.

Hanani's imprisonment for an unwelcome true word forms one more thread. He is silenced, in effect, simply for refusing to tell Asa what he wanted to hear, a pattern of costly truth telling that runs through every prophet Israel ever silenced and comes to its fullest expression in Christ, whom John describes as having come to His own, and His own did not receive Him, John 1:11. The rejection Hanani suffers in miniature, Christ absorbs completely.

Finally, Asa's failure to seek the LORD even in mortal illness stands as the clearest negative space Christ fills. Where a king with every resource still shut God out of his own dying, Christ is the physician who cannot be shut out because He is the one who comes looking for the sick rather than waiting to be summoned, Mark 2:17, and who welcomes even a dying thief's simple request, remember me, into paradise that same day, Luke 23:42 to 43. Asa's story ends with a man who would not seek; Christ's story is built entirely around a God who will not stop seeking.
study.god:
God's readiness to show Himself strong on behalf of the fully devoted, verse 9, is not a new promise invented for this crisis; it describes His settled character, active and searching rather than passive, watching the whole earth the way a patrol watches a border, alert for any heart genuinely turned toward Him. That same God had already proven this exact readiness for Asa personally, delivering him from the Cushites, which is precisely what makes Hanani's rebuke sting, not a general theological claim but a specific, remembered fact about God's own past faithfulness to this particular king.

He is also patient with process rather than demanding instant, permanent perfection, yet He does not remove the real consequences that follow misplaced trust. Hanani's warning, from now on you will be at war, verse 9, is not petty punishment for a single lapse; it is the natural unraveling of the peace faithful reliance had secured, God allowing Asa to experience, in real historical terms, exactly what trusting something other than Him actually produces.

His holiness extends even to how correction is received. Asa's rage and imprisonment of Hanani do not provoke an immediate visible judgment in the text, yet the narrative's silence is its own comment; God does not force repentance, and He allows a hardened response to run its own course toward a final illness met with the same stubbornness that met the prophet.

And He remains, even here, the God who could have been sought. The tragedy of Asa's ending is not that God became unreachable but that Asa stopped reaching, seeking physicians rather than the One who had already proven Himself willing to heal far worse than diseased feet. Nothing in the chapter suggests the door had closed; the record simply shows a king who no longer knocked on it. For worship, this leaves a sober but not hopeless lesson, that the God who once delivered dramatically remains just as reachable in the smaller, later crises, and that refusing to seek Him costs a nation and a king far more than any single lost battle ever could.

crossReferences.note: Kings records the same conflict with Baasha and the same alliance with Ben-hadad almost verbatim, though without Hanani's confrontation, showing the Chronicler working from shared royal records while adding the prophetic commentary that explains, rather than merely reports, why Asa's later reign turned out as it did.

Asa's earlier prayer against the Cushites, LORD, there is no one besides You to help, supplies the exact standard Hanani later measures him against; reading the two battles side by side is what makes verse 8's rebuke land with its full force.

Hanani's own son Jehu later confronts Jehoshaphat for allying with the house of Ahab in strikingly similar terms, should you help the wicked and love those who hate the LORD, showing one prophetic family holding two successive kings of Judah to the same exacting standard.

The same verb translated angry in verse 10 elsewhere describes divine fury against covenant rebellion, an unsettling echo that leaves Asa's rage against a faithful prophet sounding less like righteous indignation and more like the very wrath Scripture usually reserves for those who oppose God.

Zechariah later uses nearly the same image, the eyes of the LORD which range through all the earth, applied to God's attentive care over a struggling postexilic community rebuilding the temple, extending the assurance Hanani gives Asa into a very different, later crisis of discouragement.

Paul mentions Luke, the beloved physician, traveling as a trusted companion without a hint of censure, evidence that Scripture nowhere treats medical care itself as opposed to faith, which sharpens exactly what verse 12 is actually condemning in Asa, exclusivity rather than the physicians themselves.

Jesus describes His own mission using the very category Asa neglected, it is not the healthy who need a physician, but the sick, presenting Himself as the true source of healing that a dying king sought everywhere except where it could actually be found.

Ahaz later repeats Asa's exact mistake on a larger scale, stripping the temple to buy Assyrian help instead of trusting the LORD, and receiving only further distress for it, confirming that Asa's later years established a pattern of failure later kings would tragically repeat rather than learn from.

Jesus promises that the Father who sees in secret will reward what is done in secret, echoing Hanani's claim that God's eyes actively search the earth for genuine devotion, now grounded in Christ's own intimate knowledge of how closely the Father actually watches.

study.oneStory:
Asa's later years belong to that long, sobering middle stretch of the biblical story where even genuinely faithful people keep discovering that yesterday's trust does not automatically secure today's obedience. The fall in Eden was, at its root, a failure of trust, believing that God's provision was not quite enough and reaching for something else; Asa's later reign replays that same basic failure on a smaller, more personal scale, a king who had once trusted God completely now reaching for a foreign king's silver bought help instead.

What makes the chapter more than a simple morality tale is how honestly it tracks the cost of that shift. Peace gives way to war, verse 9's from now on, a faithful messenger is imprisoned rather than heeded, and a king who once cried out to God in crisis dies having sought everyone except Him. Chronicles does not soften this; the closing formula that normally credits a king's positive legacy here simply notes his burial with unusual detail about spices and fire, leaving the theological verdict to stand exactly where Hanani left it.

Yet the story is not left without hope, because it is not the final word on reliance in Chronicles. Hanani's own son confronts the next king for the same failure, and later kings like Hezekiah will show that the same test can be passed rather than failed, refusing every alternative to trust in the LORD alone even facing an empire's army, 2 Chronicles 32:7 to 8. The pattern Asa breaks, other faithful figures in the story go on to keep.

Ultimately the whole arc points toward one who never had a later, weaker chapter to His story, Christ, whose reliance on the Father never wavered from beginning to end, and who offers Himself as the physician every dying king, and every dying reader, actually needs. Where Asa's story ends in an unhealed man who would not seek, the gospel ends in an open invitation to the very physician he refused, still standing ready to be sought.

sermon.title: Asa's Folly
sermon.why: Preached August 18, 1991 on 2 Chronicles 16, this message from Desiring God works directly through Asa's later reliance on Ben-hadad instead of the LORD, drawing out exactly the contrast this study highlights between Asa's earlier faith and his later folly.

quiz.q: How did Asa respond to Baasha's fortification of Ramah?

options.text: He took silver and gold from the temple and palace treasuries and paid Ben-hadad of Aram to break his treaty with Baasha and attack Israel instead.
options.note: Verses 2-4 describe this exact response.

options.text: He cried out to the LORD in prayer as he had done against Zerah.
options.note: This is precisely what Hanani rebukes Asa for failing to do this time, in contrast to his earlier response to Zerah.

options.text: He immediately surrendered to Baasha without resistance.
options.note: Asa took decisive action, but through a foreign alliance rather than surrender or reliance on the LORD.

options.text: The chapter records no response from Asa.
options.note: Verses 2-6 detail Asa's response in full.

quiz.q: What was Hanani's central criticism of Asa's actions?

options.text: That Asa relied on the king of Aram rather than on the LORD, unlike his earlier reliance on God against the vast Cushite army.
options.note: Verses 7-8 make this exact comparison and criticism.

options.text: That Asa had not built enough fortified cities.
options.note: Hanani's criticism concerns misplaced reliance, not insufficient fortification, which Asa had already done extensively.

options.text: That Asa had failed to remove any idols from Judah.
options.note: Asa had removed many idols earlier, chapters 14-15; Hanani's rebuke concerns this specific incident of relying on Aram.

options.text: The text records no criticism of Asa from Hanani.
options.note: Verses 7-9 record an extended, specific rebuke.

quiz.q: How did Asa respond to Hanani's rebuke?

options.text: He became enraged, imprisoned the seer, and oppressed some of the people at the same time.
options.note: Verse 10 records this exact, troubling response.

options.text: He humbled himself immediately, as he had done after Shemaiah's earlier rebuke of Rehoboam's Judah.
options.note: The opposite occurred; Asa reacted with anger and imprisonment rather than humility.

options.text: He rewarded Hanani for his honesty.
options.note: Asa imprisoned Hanani rather than rewarding him, a stark contrast to a humble response.

options.text: The chapter records no reaction from Asa at all.
options.note: Verse 10 explicitly describes his angry reaction.

quiz.q: What happened during Asa's final illness?

options.text: He became severely diseased in his feet, and even then he sought only physicians, not the LORD.
options.note: Verse 12 records this exact detail.

options.text: He immediately turned to the LORD in prayer for healing.
options.note: The text explicitly states the opposite; he sought only physicians, not the LORD.

options.text: He recovered fully and reigned many more years.
options.note: The text states he died in the forty-first year of his reign, shortly after the onset of this illness, not that he recovered and reigned on.

options.text: The chapter gives no details about Asa's final illness.
options.note: Verses 12-13 give specific detail about his illness and death.

quiz.q: What does Hanani say about the LORD's eyes, and what does it mean?

options.text: That the eyes of the LORD roam over all the earth to show Himself strong on behalf of those whose hearts are fully devoted to Him.
options.note: Verse 9 gives this exact statement, emphasizing that God actively seeks out and strengthens devoted hearts.

options.text: That God is unaware of events happening on earth.
options.note: The statement affirms the opposite, God's constant, active attentiveness across the whole earth.

options.text: That God only watches Israel and ignores the rest of the world.
options.note: The text specifically says His eyes roam over all the earth, not Israel alone.

options.text: The chapter contains no statement about God's attentiveness.
options.note: Verse 9 explicitly makes this statement.

questions: Asa once relied wholly on God against overwhelming odds but later trusted a foreign alliance against a lesser threat. Where might you be tempted to trust in your own past faithfulness rather than actively relying on God today?
Hanani's rebuke was true but hard to hear, and Asa responded with anger rather than humility. How do you typically respond when someone lovingly confronts you with an uncomfortable truth?
Hanani declared that God's eyes roam the earth to strengthen the fully devoted. What would it look like for your heart to be more fully devoted to God this week, in ways only He would see?
Even in his final illness, Asa sought physicians but not the LORD. Where do you turn first when you are in crisis, and is God included in that first response?

This story is a sober warning that past faithfulness does not guarantee present faithfulness. What practices help you keep seeking God freshly and consistently, rather than resting on how you have trusted Him before?

translationNotes.note: The thirty-sixth year of Asa's reign creates a chronological difficulty, since Baasha's death is dated earlier in 1 Kings 16:8; many scholars understand years in this section as reckoned from the division of the kingdom under Rehoboam rather than from Asa's own accession.
Forms of the Hebrew word berit, covenant, appear twice in this verse, translated here as treaty, referring to the political agreement Asa invokes with Ben-hadad rather than a covenant with the LORD.
The text's pointed contrast, he did not seek the LORD but only the physicians, critiques Asa's exclusive reliance on human help rather than condemning medical treatment as inherently wrong.
